Chapter 9. Facing Yourself: Admitting, Regretting, and Rebuilding Life.
As the years go by, the weight of the past can feel impossible to shake off. Have you ever noticed how old memories sometimes sneak up and make you question your choices? For a lot of people who worked in the system, facing what they’ve done becomes something they just can’t avoid—whether that means admitting mistakes, or trying to make up for them.
Picture this: one day, someone sits alone, replaying their life since joining the organization. It’s never easy to be honest with yourself, is it? Especially when it comes to things you've done, or even just stood by and watched.
Now, admitting what happened doesn’t always mean going public. Most of the time, it’s a private struggle. One night, for example, a worker wrote a letter to an old friend, apologizing for something that happened years ago. He never sent the letter—but just writing it brought him a little peace. In that moment, he realized that facing yourself is really the first step to letting go of guilt.
Some people try to make amends by helping others. Take this story: one former member decided to share secret information with human rights organizations, even though it put him at great risk. Making that choice wasn’t easy—at first, he lived in constant fear of being found out. But gradually, he started to feel like his life had a new purpose, like he was finally paying back a debt he owed.
Rebuilding your life after leaving the system? That’s a whole different challenge. Many folks feel isolated, struggling to fit back into ordinary society. Imagine trying to start a brand new job, only to notice the wary looks people give you—almost as if your past is following you everywhere. It’s tough. And that’s when it hits you: moving on takes a lot of time, patience, and sometimes, forgiveness—not just from others, but from yourself too.
Still, there are those who manage to break free from the past. I’m reminded of one story where a former worker was able to start fresh in a distant city. He got married, had kids, and slowly built a new life. Sure, he never forgot what he’d been through, but he learned how to forgive himself and begin again. In the evenings, he'd sit with his family, telling stories about courage and making hard choices—never sharing the painful details, but always teaching lessons he’d learned.
So, what’s the big takeaway here? Facing yourself and admitting your mistakes—that’s really where freedom starts. A lot of people get stuck in regret, but some find a way to turn their pain into a fresh beginning. And maybe, just maybe, that’s the bravest thing you can do.
